meta.blurb: Every morning you wake up with a purse holding twenty-four fresh hours, and no one can take them or add to them. Arnold Bennett's cheerful little guide from 1908 shows how an ordinary, busy person can really live them.
meta.bible: Arnold Bennett: English novelist and writer (1867 to 1931) who published How to Live on 24 Hours a Day in 1908. The book's big picture: each morning your purse is filled with twenty-four hours, the unmanufactured tissue of the universe of your life; it is a daily miracle, no one can take it, no one gets more or less, you cannot borrow from tomorrow or fall into debt. His ideas, retold: make a small plan and do not try to do too much; expect to fail sometimes and begin again; the timetable is a servant, not a master; train and control the mind by concentrating on one thing; use the journey to work for thinking; the reflective mood, asking what we are doing and why; Marcus Aurelius as an example of a wise writer to think about; give the daily job full attention; about ninety minutes, three evenings a week, for a regular serious study; the arts and serious reading; nothing in life is humdrum; dangers to avoid, such as becoming a prig, boasting, or being unkind to family; try it honestly. Voice and tone: cheerful, practical, kind, friendly, like a wise neighbour; the book is over a century old and written for ordinary workers.

B1B2: Arnold Bennett was an English novelist, and in 1908 he published a small book called How to Live on 24 Hours a Day. It is a friendly guide for anyone who feels that time is slipping away.
Bennett begins with a picture: every morning you wake up and find that your purse has been filled with twenty-four hours. He calls this a daily miracle, because the supply of time never fails.
Nobody can take these hours away from you, and no one receives either more or less than you do. A king and a clerk, a rich woman and a poor one all begin each day with exactly the same amount.
You cannot borrow hours from tomorrow, so you can never fall into debt with time. You can only waste the hours that are passing now, and tomorrow's hours are kept safe for you.
Most people say that they have no time, but Bennett thinks that this is not quite true. They have as much time as anyone else, and what they lack is a good way of using it.
The hours of the working day are often decided by an employer. Bennett says that the other hours of the day belong to us, and what we do with them is our own affair.
He does not want us to rush through each day and just get to the end of it. He wants us to live every day, and to enjoy it as it passes.
Many people feel a quiet unhappiness, because they know they could be using their time better. They do their duty every day, but they feel that real life is passing them by.
Bennett says that the way to begin is to make a small and definite plan. Decide to do one useful thing each day, and then do it.
A common mistake comes soon after the first burst of excitement. A new beginner wants to do far too much, and then he is tired and discouraged within a week.
Bennett advises us to keep the plan modest, at least for the first few weeks. It is much better to succeed in a small plan than to fail in a large one.
He also tells us to expect that we will sometimes fail. One bad day does not prove that the plan is wrong, so the best answer is to start again.
A timetable should be a good servant, and it should never become a hard master. If we become slaves to the plan, we lose the joy that it was meant to give.
If you forget your plan for a day, do not feel that everything is lost. Begin again the next morning, because the habit is built from many small returns.
The hardest task, Bennett says, is to control our own minds. We want to think about one thing, but our thoughts jump away at once to something else.
He says the mind often acts like a servant that will not obey orders. It wanders off whenever we are not watching, and it often goes toward worries and silly daydreams.
The answer, he says, is practice, just as with any other skill. Start by thinking about one thing for a very short time each day, and then slowly make the time longer.
Bennett has a useful idea about when and where to practise this skill. The journey to work, which many people spend looking out of the window, could become a quiet time for thinking.
Choose one idea to think about, for example a short line from a wise writer such as Marcus Aurelius. Think about what it means and how it could change your day.
At first, your mind will run away after a few seconds. Do not be angry with it, but bring it back gently, because every return makes you stronger.
Bennett also asks us to stop sometimes and look at our own lives. We should ask ourselves what we are doing, and why we are doing it.
He calls this the reflective mood, and he says that most people hardly ever enter it. A good question to ask is what we really want most from life.
We can also think about how we treated other people today. Were we kind, honest and fair, or did we act without thinking?
A trained mind is useful in every part of life. Even the most ordinary job is done better by someone who can think clearly and keep his attention steady.
The daily job is part of life too, and it deserves our full attention. Bennett does not want us to give the best of our minds only to our free hours.
For the evenings, Bennett suggests a regular study on three nights a week. Each session should last about ninety minutes, and it should be about something that really interests you.
Ninety minutes is not too long, so a tired person can keep it up. Bennett believes that regular small efforts are worth more than rare big ones.
He says to choose something that interests you, such as music, painting or literature. These arts can give pleasure for the rest of a person's life.
Many people say that they love the arts, but they have never really studied them. Bennett believes that true enjoyment needs some effort, just like any other skill.
Reading is one of the best ways to use the evening hours. A good book should be read slowly and with full attention, and not when we are almost asleep.
Bennett is a novelist, and he does not look down on light stories. But he says that a person who reads only easy novels is not training the mind very much.
When we read, we should try to understand the ideas and not just move our eyes along the lines. A pencil, a notebook and a quiet corner can help us.
Thinking about what we have read, for example on the way home, doubles its value. The ideas then stay with us longer, because we have used them.
Bennett also says that nothing in life is truly dull when we look at it with interest. Even a short walk to the station can show us something worth noticing.
Take an interest in the people around you and in the work that they do. Every face on a bus has a story, and every job has its own skill.
Near the end, Bennett lists some dangers that a person should avoid. The first is to become proud of your plan, and to lecture other people about how they should live.
Do not boast about your new plan to everyone you meet. Quiet changes are usually the best, and the results will show for themselves.
Another danger is being rude to family and friends because of your new plan. Your friends have their own lives, and they should not suffer because you are busy improving yours.
A plan should bring more joy into your life, and not less. If it makes you gloomy and stiff and tired, then it needs to change soon.
The plan does not have to be perfect, and it can be changed as you learn. The most important thing is to begin, and to keep on beginning each time you stop.
Bennett does not want us to agree with him and then forget about it. He wants us to test his ideas honestly in our own lives and see what happens.
Small pieces of time are easy to waste, but they are also very valuable. A few minutes spent waiting for a train or a friend could be used for thinking, and they would cost nothing.
Being busy from morning to night is not the same as living well. A person can be busy all day and still feel that nothing important has happened.
After a few weeks, a new habit begins to feel natural. What once took a great effort will start to carry you along by itself.
Slowly, the person who follows a plan like this feels calmer and more satisfied. The vague feeling that life is being wasted becomes weaker and weaker.
Bennett wrote for ordinary people who have jobs, families and only a little free time. His advice is meant to work even when a person's energy is small.
We cannot make the day longer, but we can make it richer. The aim is not to do more things, but to live more of each hour.
To sum up, Bennett suggests a day with a plan, a trained mind and some time for reflection. In the evenings there should be a study that you enjoy, and an open interest in the world.
Remember the picture of the purse at the start of the book. Tomorrow morning it will be filled again with twenty-four fresh hours, and nobody can take them from you.
So the best moment to begin, Bennett would say, is today. Choose one small plan, start it gently, and enjoy the daily miracle of a new set of hours.
C1C2: Arnold Bennett, a prolific English novelist and journalist, published How to Live on 24 Hours a Day in 1908, and it was written with the busy city worker in mind. The book is short, brisk and practical, in the manner of a friend who has thought about a problem and wishes to share the result. Its subject is the oldest shortage in the world, which is not money or talent but time.

Bennett opens with a remarkable image: every morning, he says, you wake to find your purse miraculously filled with twenty-four hours, the unmanufactured tissue of the universe of your life. No one has to earn this gift, apply for it or beg for it, and it arrives again at dawn without fail. The supply of time, he concludes, is a daily miracle, though most of us have grown too used to it to notice.

This miracle is also strictly fair, since no one can take your hours from you and no one receives either more or less than you do. The duke and the dustman, the genius and the idler, all start the morning with an identical allowance. What differs between them is only the use that each makes of what has been given.

Time cannot be hoarded, and it cannot be borrowed from the future, so a person can never fall into debt with it. He can only waste the hour that is passing, and tomorrow's twenty-four are kept safe, quite untouched, until the morning comes. For that reason there is never any point in grieving over lost days, though there is every point in using the present one.

When people complain that they have no time, Bennett suspects that something else is meant, because everybody has exactly as much time as there is. What they lack is not hours but a deliberate way of spending them, and they drift through the days in a kind of comfortable fog. The first step toward a better life, therefore, is to admit that the complaint has been misplaced.

Most adults, he notes, spend a large part of the day at work, and the hours of employment are usually fixed by someone else. But the remaining hours, whatever their number, belong to the person himself, and it is there that the question of how to live is truly asked. Bennett finds it remarkable that so many people treat those free hours as an afterthought.

He is not asking us to hurry, and he says so more than once in the course of the book. The aim is not to cram more activities into the day until the calendar is bursting, but to live each day fully, tasting it as it passes rather than merely getting to the end of it. A person who rushes from task to task without attending to any may be busy, yet he is hardly alive.

Bennett describes a vague unhappiness that visits many conscientious people, a feeling that, although they do their duty each day, real life is somehow going on elsewhere. They sense that their abilities are sleeping and that their evenings are leaking away in trifles. It is this restless dissatisfaction, he thinks, that a good plan for the day can cure.

To begin, he advises the reader to draw up a small and definite plan and to commit to it with some firmness. Decide on one useful thing to be done each day, he says, and then actually do it, since a modest promise kept is worth more than a grand one forgotten. The act of keeping faith with oneself, in small matters first, is itself the first and best lesson of all.

A common hazard follows hard upon the first flush of enthusiasm: the beginner wants to do far too much, drawing up a programme that no mortal could carry out. Within a week he is exhausted and discouraged, and he abandons the whole enterprise as a failure. Bennett, who understood human nature rather well, warns his readers firmly and repeatedly against this particular error.

He therefore recommends modesty, at least for the first weeks, and urges us to prefer a small scheme that succeeds to a large one that collapses. Success, once tasted, encourages further success, whereas a failure at the outset can darken every attempt that follows. The tortoise, in other words, usually reaches the end of this particular road before the hare.

Bennett also asks us to expect that we shall sometimes fail, and to prepare ourselves for the disappointment instead of being surprised by it. A single bad day does not prove that the plan is mistaken, and it need not lead to a gloomy surrender. The right reply to a lapse is simply to begin again, with no lecture to oneself and no delay.

A timetable, he insists, ought to be a good servant, and it must never be allowed to turn into a hard master. If we become its slaves, we lose the very freedom and pleasure that it was designed to bring. The plan exists for the sake of the person, and not the person for the sake of the plan.

Should you forget your plan for a day or a week, do not conclude that everything is lost. Begin again the next morning, because a habit is not a single heroic act but the sum of countless modest returns. The man who comes back a hundred times has, in the end, never really left.

The hardest task of all, Bennett says, is the control of one's own mind, which is the instrument with which every other task is performed. We resolve to think about a single matter, yet our thoughts leap at once to some unrelated worry or idle fancy. Until that instrument is brought under reasonable command, he suggests, every other effort will be only half effective.

The mind, he says, too often behaves like a servant who refuses orders: it wanders off whenever our attention is relaxed, and it tends to stray toward anxieties and trivial daydreams. We should not be surprised by this, since few of us have ever asked it to do anything else. A faculty that has never been trained can hardly be blamed for being wild.

The remedy, Bennett argues, is practice, in the same way that a muscle or a skill is improved by regular exercise. One begins by fixing the mind on a single subject for a very short time each day, and then slowly extends the period as the strength grows. There is nothing mysterious about the method, though there is a good deal of patience required.

For the place and the hour of this training, he has a happy suggestion. The daily journey to work, which most people spend gazing from a window or glancing over a newspaper, can be turned into a quiet period of concentration. Time that was formerly lost in transit then becomes some of the most valuable time of the day.

He recommends choosing one idea to think about, such as a short passage from a wise writer like Marcus Aurelius, and turning it over carefully in the mind. What does it mean, and how might it alter the way one behaves before the day is out? The exercise is not a lesson to be memorised, but a seed to be allowed time to grow.

At the beginning, the mind will escape within a few seconds, and the beginner may feel foolish at how weak his command is. Bennett counsels a patient rather than an angry response: bring the thoughts back gently, again and again, for every return is a small victory. Nobody becomes strong in a single day, and the habit of recovery matters more than the absence of failure.

Bennett further invites us to pause now and then and look squarely at our own lives, a practice that he calls the reflective mood. We should ask ourselves what we are doing, and why we are doing it, instead of letting each day pour into the next without inspection. Few of us, he suggests, ever set aside even a quarter of an hour for such honest self-examination.

Reflection, in his hands, has a very practical purpose: to ask what we really want most from life and whether our daily habits are leading toward it. A man may discover that he has been walking steadily in a direction he never chose. To find this out early is an enormous gift, for the road can still be changed.

We may reflect, too, upon our conduct toward other people, asking whether we were kind, honest and fair in the course of the day, or whether we acted from sheer thoughtlessness. Such questions carry no punishment and no shame, only a clearer and kinder view of ourselves than we usually have. A person who looks honestly at his own behaviour is already on the way to improving it.

A trained mind is an asset in every corner of life, and even the humblest occupation is done better by someone who can think clearly and keep his attention steady. The faculties that are exercised in the evening do not stay behind when the morning comes. In this sense the private discipline of the mind is the best investment that a working person can make.

The daily job, Bennett says, is a part of life too, and it deserves our energy and interest, not merely the leftovers of our attention. It would be a poor bargain to give the best of the mind only to the free hours and to carry a sleepwalker's mind into the office. A day is not divided into living and not living, but is lived from end to end.

For the evenings, Bennett makes a firm suggestion: three nights a week, for about ninety minutes each time, one should follow a regular and serious study of a chosen subject. The sum of these hours, over many months, is astonishing, though no single evening feels heroic. The proposal is not to abandon pleasure, but to claim a modest portion of the week for steady growth.

Ninety minutes, he reasons, is short enough to be kept up by a tired person after a long day, and long enough to achieve something real. The principle behind the figure is regularity, since he believes that small efforts repeated faithfully are worth more than rare and splendid bursts. Steadiness, and not speed, is the quality that he wishes above all to teach his readers.

The question that follows is what the student ought to choose, and Bennett urges that it be something that truly interests him, and he places the arts high on the list, among them music, painting and literature. They can offer pleasure for the rest of a person's life, and their delights deepen with every year of attention. A subject chosen from duty alone will not hold; one chosen from curiosity will.

Many people proclaim that they love the arts, he observes, yet have never made the effort of studying them, and so their enjoyment remains thin and accidental. Real appreciation, he believes, must be earned, just like skill in a game or a trade. Whoever is willing to do the work finds that a symphony or a poem opens like a door that has long been shut.

Reading, in Bennett's view, is among the best uses of the evening, but it should be done properly. A serious book ought to be read slowly and with full attention, and not at midnight when we are half asleep and ready to be overcome by the first comfortable paragraph. Good books, like good friends, reward the reader who arrives awake and ready to give them his attention.

Bennett, himself a novelist, has no quarrel with light stories, and he enjoys them as much as anyone. But a person who reads nothing except easy novels, he says, is hardly training his mind at all, for the effort that makes a mind strong is exactly what such reading avoids. Pleasure and discipline can sit comfortably together, but they should never be confused with each other.

When we read seriously, we should try to grasp the argument and the feeling of the writer, and not merely let our eyes travel along the lines. A pencil, a notebook and a quiet corner may help us to hold on to what we find. The aim is understanding, which is a different thing from having turned the pages.

To think over what we have read, perhaps during the journey home, is to double its value. The ideas then settle into the mind and become part of it, since we have turned them over and tested them, rather than merely passed them by. A book that is read once and forgotten is worth far less than a book that is read and then thought about.

Bennett also claims that nothing in life is truly humdrum for a person who looks at it with interest. Even a short walk to the station, he suggests, can offer something worth noticing, whether it is a face, a sound or the light on a wall. Boredom, on this view, is less a fact about the world than a habit of the eye.

Take a genuine interest, he says, in the people around you and in the work that they do. Every face on a bus has a story folded inside it, and every trade has its own skill and its own small triumphs. The world is a good deal more crowded with wonder than a tired and hurried mind is ever willing to admit.

Near the end of the book, Bennett warns of the dangers that attend the new way of living, and the first of them is to become a prig. This is the person who grows so proud of his plan that he lectures all his friends about how they ought to spend their own hours. Nothing, Bennett implies, spoils a good habit so quickly or so completely as a long and self-satisfied sermon.

A related fault is to boast of the scheme to everyone one meets, as if the telling were part of the doing. Quiet changes are the most lasting, he suggests, and the results will in time show for themselves, without any trumpet. The best evidence that a plan is working is that other people begin to ask how you manage.

Another danger lies in becoming unkind to family and friends on account of the new plan. Those around us have their own lives and their own claims, and they ought not to be neglected or made to suffer because we are busy improving ours. A self-improvement that costs us our warmth toward other people has, in the end, improved nothing at all.

A good plan, Bennett says, should bring more joy into a life, and certainly not less of it. If it makes a person gloomy, stiff and anxious, then it is a poor plan, and it needs to be loosened, shortened or changed. What Bennett wants is a cheerful and willing discipline, and not a grim and joyless drill carried out for its own sake.

The scheme need not be perfect, and it can be revised as experience teaches. The most important matter, he says, is simply to begin, and to keep beginning each time the thread is broken. There is more wisdom in a clumsy start than in a flawless design that remains forever on paper.

Bennett does not want his readers to agree with him and then forget the whole business. He wants them to put his ideas to an honest test in their own lives, to watch what happens, and to judge the results with their own eyes. A suggestion that is never tried, after all, can teach nothing to the person who read it and agreed.

Small pieces of time are easily wasted, yet they are also very valuable, for they are scattered through every day like loose change. A few minutes spent waiting for a train, a meeting or a friend could be given to a thought or a page, and the price would be nothing. Added together over the course of a whole year, those small minutes form a surprisingly large fortune.

Being busy from morning to night is not the same as living well, Bennett reminds us, and a person may rush through his hours and still feel that nothing important has happened. The question to ask is not how much has been done, but how much of the day was truly lived. Quality of attention, rather than quantity of activity, is the measure that he proposes.

After a few weeks, a new habit begins to feel natural, and what once demanded a great deal of effort starts to carry the person along by itself. The early struggle is the price of the later ease, and it is a fair price. Many who have given up too soon have given up just before the road became smooth.

Slowly the person who follows a plan like this grows calmer and more satisfied, and the vague sense that life is being wasted weakens and fades. His days begin to have a shape, and he no longer feels like a passenger on a train whose destination he never chose. It is a quiet change, and it comes without any fuss, but few changes are more welcome to the person who feels it.

Bennett wrote for ordinary people who have jobs, families and only a small stock of leisure, and he understood that their energy at the end of the day was limited. His advice is therefore meant to work even when a person is tired and hurried, which is exactly when most advice fails. That practical sympathy for the tired reader is a large part of the charm and the lasting usefulness of the book.

We cannot lengthen the day, but we can make it richer, and this is the deepest point of the book. The aim is not to do more things, but to live more of each hour, with a mind that is awake and a heart that is interested. A person who learns this has found something far better than any cunning time-saving trick or clever device.

To sum up, Bennett proposes a day that has a modest plan, a trained mind and a little time for reflection. In the evenings there is a regular study that one enjoys, and throughout the day there is an open interest in the world and its people. None of this requires money, talent or luck, but only the plain decision to begin on some ordinary morning.

Recall the picture with which the book began, of the purse that is filled each morning with twenty-four hours. Tomorrow it will be filled again, and nobody on earth can take the hours from you or add one more to your neighbour's. What happens to those hours depends, as it always has depended, upon nobody but the person who holds the purse.

The best moment to begin, Bennett would say, is today, and the best way to begin is small. Choose one modest plan, hold it lightly, and return to it whenever you forget, taking pleasure in the plain miracle of a fresh set of hours. The book is more than a century old, yet the purse is still filled each morning, and the choice is as open as ever.
